Will Missouri force enough turnovers to materially disrupt Miami’s preferred rim/entry offense (e.g., win the turnover battle by a meaningful margin)?
A) Yes—Missouri forces at least a modest turnover edge (relative to Miami’s 11.2/game baseline) that converts into direct offense or prolonged possessions, limiting Miami’s paint-centric half-court flow.
B) No—Missouri does not meaningfully win the turnover battle; Miami protects the ball enough that Missouri’s disruption fails to break Miami’s scoring rhythm.

Will Miami’s defense limit opponent second-half scoring efficiency (a sustained “defensive lock”)?
A) Yes—Missouri’s shooting/points after halftime are meaningfully worse than before halftime.
B) No—Missouri’s second-half output is not materially suppressed; the defensive edge isn’t sustained.

Will Missouri’s defense force Miami into more contested perimeter attempts (e.g., fewer clean paint entries)?
A) Yes—Missouri forces Miami to take a higher share of difficult jumpers due to reduced post-entry quality.
B) No—Miami continues to get its preferred paint pressure and direct rim actions regularly.

Will Udeh Jr. stay on the floor and avoid foul trouble affecting rim protection?
A) Yes—Udeh avoids significant foul trouble, preserving his shot-contest impact.
B) No—Udeh accumulates fouls or is forced into limited minutes/contests that reduce rim deterrence.

Which team wins the rebounding battle by at least a small margin (e.g., +2 or better) overall?
A) Miami wins the overall rebounding margin (especially defensive board control), limiting second-chance points and preventing Missouri from extending possessions offensively.
B) Missouri wins or matches Miami strongly on the glass (e.g., +2 or better), allowing extra possessions via offensive rebounds and keeping Missouri close or ahead on possession volume.

Statistical matchup: Will Miami’s defense hold Missouri’s shooting to an efficiency level consistent with Missouri’s season allowing weaker-than-average offensive outputs (i.e., enough to keep Missouri below its usual scoring/efficiency baseline)?
A) Yes. Miami’s man-to-man/positional defense plus Udeh rim protection will limit Missouri’s eFG% to roughly the low end of what Missouri typically allows, keeping Missouri’s offense from operating at its usual 116-ish points/100-possessions (or equivalent efficiency level).
B) No. Missouri will get enough efficient looks (drive-and-kick threes and closeouts) that its shot quality stays near its season offensive efficiency, so Miami will not suppress Missouri to a materially below-baseline scoring/efficiency outcome.

What is the effective three-point outcome for each team in this single game (not season averages)—does the shooting variance favor Missouri’s perimeter shotmakers or neutralize Miami’s secondary spacing?
A) Missouri’s three-point shooting is high enough (e.g., Stone/Crews/Pierce shooting above their typical efficiency) that they can punish any Miami shell/paint help.
B) Missouri’s three-point shooting is average-to-below average, so Miami’s interior control and post/rim offense face less perimeter punishment and Miami can pack the paint more safely.

Will Missouri keep Miami’s 3-point shooting below Miami’s typical make rate (i.e., suppresses makes enough to matter), rather than allowing open-volume threes?
A) Yes. Missouri’s perimeter defense holds Miami’s made threes well below what Miami needs for a comfortable lead (contested/limited attempts and/or low makes).
B) No. Missouri allows enough quality looks from three that Miami’s shooting variance flips—Miami makes a meaningful number of threes and gains cushion from distance.

Will Mark Mitchell’s shot profile include enough high-value shot-making (not overly contested or off-balance)?
A) Yes—Mitchell gets enough efficient looks (or creates foul/FT opportunities) to sustain offense.
B) No—Mitchell’s looks are consistently low-quality (contested, forced passouts, or poor shot selection).

Will Missouri’s key wing perimeter shooters (e.g., Stone/Pierce/Crews) collectively hit enough threes to keep Miami’s defense from overloading the interior?
A) Yes—at least two of the perimeter creators deliver above/at-baseline three-point making that forces Miami to respect kick-out spacing.
B) No—perimeter three-point performance falls below baseline so Miami can crowd paint entries without being punished.

Will Miami’s second-chance/paint damage translate into a clear paint-points advantage versus Missouri’s frontcourt size (i.e., Miami wins the paint battle by a noticeable margin)?
A) Yes—Miami gets consistent paint pressure and a noticeable paint-points edge (via Reneau post advantages and Udeh rebounding/vertical finish), producing a scoring margin from interior touches.
B) No—Missouri substantially walls off or contests inside, preventing a paint scoring edge; Miami’s scoring tilts away from the interior and loses that positional advantage.

Will Missouri’s defensive transition stop count (stops/deflections/contests) be high enough to reduce Miami’s transition points?
A) Yes—Missouri creates enough stops/shot contests that Miami does not score many quick points.
B) No—Miami still generates substantial transition points (or quick-pipeline scoring) off misses/steals.

How often does Missouri convert Miami turnovers and missed shots into fast-break points (i.e., does the game tilt toward Missouri’s transition offense rather than a set-play half-court grind)?
A) Yes: Missouri produces a clear run in transition off Miami’s live-ball mistakes/forced turnovers and/or rebound chances, creating a meaningful fast-break scoring advantage.
B) No: Transition remains limited—either Miami protects the glass/holds possession after misses, or Missouri fails to generate enough steals/deflections to consistently turn chaos into points.

Historical & situational: Does seeding/resume translate into a reliability advantage (e.g., Miami’s tournament-safe quadrant profile vs Missouri’s more mixed recent reliability)?
A) Yes. Miami’s more consistently “tournament-safe” body of work (better avoidance of bad losses; more Q1/Q2 stability) indicates a higher probability of performance stability in one-and-done conditions.
B) No. Missouri’s resume includes enough Q1/Q2 wins and late-game closeness that seeding-based stability arguments are overstated; Missouri’s ceiling outcomes are frequent enough that it remains a near coin-flip.

How often does Miami generate efficient high-percentage shots at the rim (or at the level of Udeh/Reneau interior scoring), rather than settling for low-percentage midrange?
A) Frequently. Miami obtains a substantial share of shots at the rim/near-rim and finishes at a rate consistent with its paint-pressure identity.
B) Infrequently. Miami’s interior looks are either blocked/contested often enough or disrupted enough that finishing efficiency collapses relative to its typical paint-dominant games.

Will Miami’s defense limit Missouri’s effective field goal quality (e.g., keep Missouri below its season offensive efficiency threshold)?
A) Yes—Miami’s positional defense and rim protection produce a defensive-efficiency outcome closer to a tournament contender (holding Missouri to a worse-than-its-season scoring efficiency).
B) No—Miami’s defense allows Missouri to achieve near-season efficiency (or better) because Missouri’s shotmaking and spacing neutralize containment.

Will the game likely be decided within one possession (tight variance) rather than by a large margin?
A) Yes—final margin is one possession or less most likely (e.g., 1–6 points).
B) No—final margin is larger (double digits) or one team clearly separates.

Does recent tournament/seeding context favor Miami’s floor more than Missouri’s volatility (i.e., the lower predictive ceiling risk for Miami manifests)?
A) Yes—Miami’s tournament-safe profile (avoiding bad losses, stable road/late competence) translates into fewer collapses; they play to their dependable identity.
B) No—Missouri’s high-variance, late-game closer profile shows up as the deciding pattern (upset script executes), overpowering Miami’s stability.

Will Missouri’s defensive “volatility” manifest as a late defensive breakdown against Miami’s half-court sets?
A) Yes—Missouri gives up late-game runs/partial collapses that Miami capitalizes on in the final minutes.
B) No—Missouri’s defense stabilizes late and prevents Miami from turning possessions into decisive runs.

Will Miami’s primary interior scorer (Malik Reneau) avoid inefficient shot outcomes through the game (measured as sustained scoring efficiency/shot quality from his primary areas)?
A) Yes—Reneau maintains efficient scoring (post/short-mid paint touches) and produces a meaningful share of Miami points through interior creation.
B) No—Reneau is forced out of his comfort zone or heavily contested and produces below his typical efficiency/role.

Will the game tempo (possessions) land closer to Miami’s preferred controlled range rather than Missouri’s pace-seeking range?
A) Yes—tempo is closer to slower/controlled, reducing Missouri’s transition volatility.
B) No—tempo opens up; possessions increase meaningfully and benefit Missouri’s run/counterattack identity.

Will Miami’s three-point shooting be above typical “just solid” levels and bail it out if paint is contested?
A) Yes—Miami knocks down enough threes to keep Missouri’s compact defense honest.
B) No—Miami’s three-point production stays mediocre/low, so contested paint becomes too costly.

Coaching & strategy: Will Dennis Gates’ ability to adjust mid-game and manage defensive intensity swings produce a second-half offensive defensive plan that changes the game state (like his known second-half surges)?
A) Yes. Gates will identify and exploit Miami’s specific vulnerabilities during the game (e.g., forcing Miami into more half-court perimeter dependence, increasing pressure/deflections at the right moments).
B) No. Gates’ adjustments won’t translate into a durable advantage; Miami’s defensive structure plus interior rim protection will prevent Missouri’s adjustments from creating sustained separation.

Coaching & strategy: Will Jai Lucas’ game-plan emphasis on disrupting the paint/post-entry timing (and managing second-half adjustments) be sufficient to neutralize Missouri’s primary scoring initiator (Mark Mitchell)?
A) Yes. Lucas will successfully alter matchups/entry timing and/or help rotations so Mitchell’s downhill creation is frequently contested or rerouted, leading to Missouri having to settle more often than it wants.
B) No. Lucas will not fully solve Mitchell’s creation—Missouri will keep finding Mitchell as a consistent late-clock engine (even if some possessions are slowed), so Missouri’s offense maintains its ability to generate efficient scoring.

Health & conditioning: Are Miami’s and Missouri’s rotation players available and not significantly limited (no major injury or foul-trouble constraints that would reduce defensive intensity or post play)?
A) Yes. Both teams enter relatively full-strength; no starter-level availability issues materially reduce minutes or effectiveness, especially in Miami’s rim/paint roles and Missouri’s primary creators/big defender.
B) No. At least one key player (for Miami: the rim/paint anchor or primary creator; for Missouri: Mitchell and/or the interior defensive presence) is limited enough to reduce performance, rotation depth, or late-game execution.
